id: A Shropshire Lad  1: From Clee to heaven the beacon burns

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

From Clee to heaven the beacon burns, The shires have seen it plain, From north and south the sign returns And beacons burn again. Look left, look right, the hills are bright, The dales are light between, Because 'tis fifty years to-night That God has saved the Queen. Now, when the flame they watch not towers About the soil they trod, Lads, we'll remember friends of ours Who shared the work with God. To skies that knit their heartstrings right, To fields that bred them brave, The saviours come not home to-night: Themselves they could not save. It dawns in Asia, tombstones show And Shropshire names are read; And the Nile spills his overflow Beside the Severn's dead. We pledge in peace by farm and town The Queen they served in war, And fire the beacons up and down The land they perished for. "God save the Queen" we living sing, From height to height 'tis heard; And with the rest your voices ring, Lads of the Fifty-third. Oh, God will save her, fear you not: Be you the men you've been, Get you the sons your fathers got, And God will save the Queen.

outputs.L1:
From Clee to heaven the beacon burns;  
The shires have seen it plain.  
From north and south the signal returns,  
And beacons blaze again.  

Look left, look right—the hills are bright,  
The dales are lit between,  
For it is fifty years tonight  
Since God has saved the Queen.  

Now, while the flames they cannot watch  
Rise above the soil they trod,  
Lads, we shall remember friends of ours  
Who shared the work with God.  

To skies that bound their heartstrings true,  
To fields that bred them brave,  
The saviours come not home tonight;  
Themselves they could not save.  

It dawns in Asia; tombstones show,  
And Shropshire names are read.  
The Nile pours out its overflow  
Beside the Severn’s dead.  

We pledge, in peace, by farm and town,  
The Queen they served in war,  
And light the beacons up and down  
The land they perished for.  

“God save the Queen,” we living sing;  
From height to height it is heard.  
And with the rest, let your voices ring,  
Lads of the Fifty-third.  

Oh, God will save her—fear you not.  
Be you the men you have been;  
Raise sons like those your fathers raised,  
And God will save the Queen.
outputs.L2:
The signal fire blazes from Clee toward the sky, and every county has clearly seen its light. From both the north and the south, answering flames rise, and the beacons are lit once more. Look to either side: the hills shine, and the valleys glow between them, for tonight marks fifty years since God preserved the Queen.

Yet now, while these flames climb above the land where they once walked, let us remember, lads, our own companions who helped carry out God’s work. They do not return tonight to the heavens that bound their loyalties so firmly, nor to the fields that raised them to be courageous. Those who helped save others are absent; they could not save themselves.

Morning breaks in Asia, where gravestones bear names from Shropshire. The Nile floods onward near the graves of men from the Severn country. In peace, beside farms and towns, we drink to the Queen whom they served in war, and we light the beacons across the nation for which they died.

We who are still alive sing, “God save the Queen,” and the cry passes from hilltop to hilltop. Let your voices join the others too, lads of the Fifty-third. Do not doubt that God will protect her: remain the kind of men you have always been, raise sons like the fathers who raised you, and God will save the Queen.
outputs.L3:
Across the shires, beacons are lit in celebration of fifty years in which God has preserved and protected the Queen. Their flames shine out over the countryside as signs of loyalty, gratitude, and national rejoicing. The people gather not only to celebrate the Queen’s long reign, but also to remember the cost at which the peace and honor of the country have often been maintained.

The poem calls upon the living to think of the friends and comrades who once served bravely but never returned home. These fallen men are not to be forgotten amid the celebrations. Though the fires burn brightly and the nation gives thanks, memory must turn to those who gave their lives in service. Their courage and sacrifice form part of the meaning of the day.

The dead are honored even in distant lands. Far from Shropshire, in places across Asia and by the Nile, their graves bear familiar Shropshire names. These names mark the resting places of men who left their homes to fight for Queen and country and who died far from the fields and villages they once knew. Their presence in foreign soil reminds the living that the empire’s service carried many sons far away, and that some paid the final price.

In peace, the people renew their pledge of loyalty to the Queen. They honor her not through battle, but through remembrance, gratitude, and faithfulness. Those who served her in war and died for their country are held up as examples of devotion. Their sacrifice deepens the people’s commitment to remain loyal in calmer times.

Finally, the poem urges the next generation to show the same firmness and courage as their fathers. If they remain steadfast, dutiful, and true, then the blessing celebrated in the beacons may continue. The hope is that God will go on saving the Queen, and that the people will prove worthy of the legacy left by those who served, suffered, and died before them.
outputs.L4:
The poem commemorates Queen Victoria’s jubilee by presenting the celebration not simply as a moment of public festivity, but as an occasion for national remembrance. It imagines beacon fires being lit across Britain, their flames joining towns, villages, and distant communities in a shared act of patriotic celebration. These fires symbolize unity and loyalty, gathering the people together around the figure of the Queen and the long reign she represents.

Yet the poem also deepens the meaning of the jubilee by turning attention to the soldiers who have died in service overseas. The national rejoicing is therefore shadowed by memory: the prosperity, stability, and glory associated with Victoria’s reign have been secured at great human cost. The poem suggests that the Queen and the nation have been “saved” through the courage, suffering, and deaths of men who fought in distant lands. Their sacrifice becomes the moral foundation of the celebration.

As a result, the poem combines imperial pride with solemn commemoration. It honors the loyalty of those who served the empire, while also insisting that their deaths must not be forgotten amid public rejoicing. The jubilee is presented as both a tribute to Queen Victoria and an act of mourning for the fallen. In this way, the poem transforms a national celebration into a memorial, reminding its readers that patriotic glory depends upon sacrifice.
outputs.L5:
From the quiet hills near Clee, the morning light spreads gently across the fields, turning the landscape gold. The village wakes slowly, with birdsong in the hedgerows and the soft sound of footsteps on old stone paths. It is a place where time seems to move at its own pace, offering peace, history, and a deep connection to the countryside.

The view from Clee is wide and calming, reminding visitors how beautiful simple places can be. Whether walking along the trails, exploring local stories, or simply watching the clouds pass over the hills, there is something memorable about the area. From its natural charm to its peaceful atmosphere, Clee leaves a lasting impression on all who visit.
